answer.question: Can I water a lawn from my Henderson well?
answer.answer: Only if your permit includes lawn and garden irrigation. A household-use-only permit rules out growing plants outside the house, and even an irrigation permit caps the area. Look yours up in the state's Well Permits search; turf needs no water.

blocks.h2: On a household-use-only well, the lawn gets nothing.
blocks.takeaway: A household-use-only well permit rules out watering a lawn at all. Look your well up in the state's search tool — artificial turf needs no water from it either way.
paras: On a Henderson well, the permit decides whether outdoor watering is allowed at all. Guideline 2023-1 spells out what a household-use-only permit excludes: growing plants anywhere outside the house, a greenhouse included, and washing vehicles, windows or decks. Watering is limited to personal plants grown indoors.
A permit that does include lawn and garden irrigation still has limits. The irrigated area is capped, and the water can't be used to fill pools, ponds, fountains or waterfalls.

Look your well up before you plan anything green. The state's Well Permits search finds a permit by address, parcel ID or permit number and shows its permitted use. If it says household use only, that well can't keep a lawn alive, and artificial turf is the green that asks nothing of it.

blocks.h2: Two groundwater systems carry Henderson addresses.
blocks.takeaway: Not every Henderson home has its own well — some are on a small community water system instead. Ask whichever system bills you whether it limits outdoor watering before you budget new grass.
paras: Not every home here has its own well. EPA drinking water records list two active community water systems at Henderson, 80640 addresses, and both draw groundwater: Hazeltine Heights Water, with 88 service connections, and Tucson WC, with 36 (checked 12 September 2026).

Neither record says anything about lawns. Ask the system that bills you whether it limits outdoor watering before you budget for new grass. Our metro rebate rundown covers the larger providers that publish their terms.

blocks.h2: Find the soil treatment area before any base is dug.
blocks.takeaway: County rules protect the ground over your leach field from compaction by traffic, recreation or site work, and a turf base is compacted rock. Ask the health department first; we place turf around its answer.
paras: Septic systems here fall under Adams County Health Department Regulation O-26, adopted on 20 November 2025 and in force since 5 January 2026 (Board of Health Resolution 2025-012). It treats the ground over the leach field as part of the system.

Section 11.10 restricts use of the surface over any part of the system. The soil treatment area must not be subject to damage or soil compaction from livestock, vehicular traffic, recreational use or other site development activity. A field built to O-26 gets at least 10 inches of final cover of soil suitable for vegetation, graded to divert storm water away.

A turf base is compacted rock, a putting green is recreation, and a dog run is traffic every day. O-26 doesn't name artificial turf, so ask the department's Water Quality team, 303-288-6816, whether turf may sit over or beside your soil treatment area. Its septic system lookup can turn up the record for your system. We place the turf around their answer.

blocks.h2: The county doesn't count artificial turf as landscaping.
blocks.takeaway: New development can't use turf as landscape material; asking for it means meeting minimum planting and requesting an alternative turf design. Turf behind an existing home is a separate case, so ask the county.
paras: Chapter 4 of Adams County's Development Standards and Regulations, in the version dated 1 October 2024, says no artificial trees, plants or turf shall be used as a landscape material. An applicant who wants artificial turf must still meet the minimum plant requirements and send the Director of Community and Economic Development a request for an alternative turf design with drainage specifications (Section 4-19-04-01).

That section reaches new development that hadn't applied for a building permit when it took effect, and existing development that needs a change in use permit. For a new single-family house outside eastern Adams County, the chapter also wants the front and side setbacks landscaped and at least 30% of the back yard. Turf behind an existing home is a separate case.
So ask before you build. The county's Planner of the Day, 720-523-6800, answers zoning questions, and Planning & Development takes zoning verification applications through its ePermit Center.

blocks.h2: Well, tank and field set the edges of the turf.
blocks.takeaway: Your well, tank and leach field set fixed points before any layout starts. We edge turf around septic lids rather than laying over them, and mark everything at the free visit.
paras: Table 6 of O-26 keeps a leach field trench or bed at least 100 feet from a well. A Henderson lot with both has fixed points before any design starts, and the turf works in the room between them and the house.

Keep the septic lids reachable. The county's Use Permit FAQ lists risers and lids below grade among the deficiencies an inspector flags, and they have to be repaired before a permit is issued. Turf edged around a lid, not laid over it, keeps that simple.

At the free visit we measure, check the ground and mark the well, the tank and any known field lines. You approve a custom layout before work starts. Then we prepare the site, build a base for your soil, lay, seam and edge the turf, add infill, finish and clean up, and walk you through the care it needs.

servicesNote: Choose a lawn, a dog run or a backyard green, laid out around the well, the tank and the leach field.

faq.q: Who installs artificial turf in Henderson, CO?
faq.a: We install artificial lawns, pet turf and backyard putting greens in Henderson, CO, on unincorporated acreage and in the parts annexed by nearby cities. On a lot with a well and a septic system, the layout starts from what the well permit allows and where the leach field sits. Call 303-349-2368 for a free visit to measure and check the ground.

faq.q: Is my Henderson address in Commerce City, Brighton or Thornton?
faq.a: It might be. Portions of the Henderson area have been annexed by Commerce City, Brighton and Thornton (Wikipedia), so a Henderson mailing address doesn't settle it. Confirm it with Adams County Planning & Development before relying on a county rule. Inside a city, that city's code and water provider apply instead: see our Commerce City, Brighton and Thornton pages.

faq.q: Does the ground change across Henderson?
faq.a: It can within a mile. USDA soil data puts Henderson's mapped coordinates on Nunn clay loam, 1 to 3 percent slopes, a fine clay soil. About a mile east, the map unit is Vona sandy loam, 0 to 1 percent slopes, a coarse, well-drained one (USDA Soil Data Access). Clay holds water and moves with it; sand drains fast and settles under load. We check your own ground and build the base for it.

faq.q: Do I need a septic inspection when I sell?
faq.a: In most cases, yes. O-26 requires an inspection report and a Use Permit dated within 12 months before a sale, a remodel that adds flow to the system, or a change in use, and the seller is the one who gets it. A certified inspector checks the tank, any controls and pumps, and the soil treatment area. A permit for a sale is valid until closing or for twelve months, whichever comes first.
